key_concept: In photorespiration, RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase, splitting RuBP ($C_5$) into one 3-phosphoglycerate ($C_3$) and one 2-phosphoglycolate ($C_2$).
steps: RuBisCO is a bifunctional enzyme. It acts as a carboxylase with $CO_2$ (Calvin cycle) and as an oxygenase with $O_2$ (photorespiration).
In the oxygenation reaction, $O_2$ binds instead of $CO_2$, so no carbon is added: $RuBP + O_2 \rightarrow$ 3-PGA $+$ 2-phosphoglycolate.
Carbon balance check: $C_5 \rightarrow C_3 + C_2$. Therefore X must be a 2-carbon compound, which is phosphoglycolate.
Phosphoglycolate then passes through the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria (the glycolate pathway). One $CO_2$ is released in the mitochondria, with no ATP or NADPH gained.
why_not_others: PEP is the 3C primary $CO_2$ acceptor in $C_4$ plants. Oxaloacetate (4C) is the first product of PEP carboxylase, and malate (4C) is formed from OAA in the $C_4$/CAM pathway. None of these is produced when RuBisCO reacts with $O_2$.
common_trap: Students confuse $C_4$-pathway intermediates (PEP, OAA, malate) with photorespiration products, or write glycolate instead of phosphoglycolate as the direct RuBisCO product.
time_saving_tip: Count carbons. RuBP has 5 C and 3-PGA has 3 C, so X must have 2 C, and only phosphoglycolate fits.
